questions.q: Per this lesson, what is the key difference between "diagnosing backward" (like Lesson 12's case study) and "designing forward" (this lesson's focus)?
options: There is no real difference between the two skills
Designing forward only applies to Apex code, never to architecture
Diagnosing backward identifies gaps in an existing design that's placed in front of you; designing forward produces a complete design from a blank requirement where nothing is labeled as a gap yet
Diagnosing backward is always easier and requires no real skill
questions.explain: The case study and incident lessons practiced finding gaps in something already built. This lesson asks for the reverse and arguably harder skill: producing a design from scratch, using the course's vocabulary deliberately rather than reacting to problems already identified for you.

questions.q: In the seven-step design method, what should come first, before any specific control is decided?
options: Deciding which fields to encrypt
Choosing between Named Principal and Per-User authentication
Writing the incident response plan
Naming every boundary in the proposed system where trust changes
questions.explain: The method starts with naming boundaries (Lesson 1) before any specific control decision, because every later step -- least privilege, depth, threat modeling, encryption -- is applied at a boundary that has to be identified first.

questions.q: Per step 3 of the method ("add depth, deliberately"), what question should be asked about each boundary's primary control?
options: What the next independent layer is if that primary control fails -- if the honest answer is "nothing," the design isn't finished yet
Whether the control is the cheapest option available
Whether the control has ever been used anywhere else in the org before
Whether the control requires a Shield license
questions.explain: This step directly applies Lesson 3's defense-in-depth mindset: assume the primary control fails, and ask what independent layer limits the damage. "Nothing" as an answer means the design still has a gap.

questions.q: What makes an answer like "we used Named Principal because that's what we always use" indefensible in a review board setting, per this lesson?
options: Named Principal is never an acceptable choice in any scenario

It states a conclusion without the reasoning a reviewer would need to actually evaluate whether the choice fits this specific case, unlike an answer that explains why the choice fits this particular integration's needs
It violates Salesforce's terms of service
It is factually incorrect regardless of context
questions.explain: A defensible design shows its reasoning, not just its conclusion. "We always use this" gives a reviewer nothing to evaluate against this specific case's actual needs -- exactly what Lesson 11's review process is meant to push back on.

questions.q: In the closing Lab's professional services portal scenario, why does the method call for running a STRIDE pass specifically on the document upload feature?
options: Because document uploads cannot be secured by any other method covered in this course
Because STRIDE only applies to billing integrations, never to document uploads

Because document upload features are explicitly a boundary where trust changes (clients, external to the org's internal boundary, are writing data in) and handle potentially sensitive financial documents, making it exactly the kind of surface this course's threat-modeling step targets
Because Health Check automatically covers document upload security, making STRIDE redundant
questions.explain: Per Lesson 5 and this lesson's method, threat modeling is aimed specifically at places where trust changes and sensitive data is handled -- a client-facing upload feature handling sensitive financial documents is exactly that kind of surface, which is why the Lab calls it out specifically rather than treating the whole portal as one undifferentiated unit.
